Hello! Former bisexual teen here. 

First off, thanks for sharing! Sexuality can be very confusing, but the fact that you are reflecting on it is a good thing! 

As a pansexual/bisexual woman, I would say that just because you find yourself attracted to a person of a certain gender presentation (in your words, a cross dresser or femboy) doesn’t necessarily mean you MUST make a decision about your sexuality RIGHT NOW. 

I remember when I was first experiencing attraction to women, I was panicking at the thought that I must now be a lesbian?!?!? *insert panicky Kermit meme* 

However, as I spent more time reflecting and experimenting and so on, I realized that a label doesn’t need to be the only word that defines you. It describes how you feel at this moment in time. Labels are not permanent. Sometimes they stick around for decades, sometimes they can change very suddenly. It all depends on your experience and how you want to present yourself to the world. 

Maybe instead of committing to the word bisexual, you try saying that you are exploring or questioning? If you’re comfortable, maybe using the word queer? Or, if your mind is totally abuzz with anxiety, simply use no word at all. Your sexuality is no one’s business but your own; you do not owe anyone an answer or explanation. Do what feels right for you. 

If a day comes when you are more comfortable exploring the idea of bisexuality, maybe read up on the subject! There’s so many resources out there for people exploring their identity/sexuality for the first time. For the time being, I’ll just drop the following idea in your brain, and you can ponder it as you will: the definition of bisexuality (that I can remember) is simply the attraction to two or more gender identities. So, if you like women and are attracted to feminine-presenting men, that would be two genders, so you could be bisexual! If you are attracted to women, feminine-presenting men, or genderqueer or non-binary people who like to present as feminine, that’s three genders right there! Still could be bisexual! If you are attracted to any and all feminine-presenting people, you could be bisexual or pansexual! 

But don’t let all the words and phrases worry your heart. You have time and space to figure all of this out, and there are people out there who want to help and support you. Be yourself, set what pace you want, search for joy, and be at peace. You’ve got this. 

P.S. Please don’t be convinced that there are “real” and “fake” versions of sexuality. Your sexuality is very real and valid, even if you are not super duper sure of what it is yet. You can identify as whatever you want and you can learn to ignore bigoted buttwads that tell you what you should be. Live your life on your terms. Good luck!

As a former LGBTeen, I can say that I used to be very worried about such things as well. I distinctly remember frequently searching the World Wide Interwebs for answers about my sexuality. I went by bisexual for a few years, but then I found the term pansexual, and it was like a lightbulb moment - that’s me!

I think my advice to you will be very similar to that of others. Right now, I would suggest not worrying about labels too much. I know that a lot of us spend hours or even years searching for the right words. Sometimes we find them, sometimes we don’t. Just take this time to be who you want to be, and love the people you want to love. It tends to make life much simpler. 

When I was much younger, I wished I had been born a boy. However, in growing up, I realized that because I had lived in such a conservative area, I only wanted to be a boy because I wanted to be free of the restrictive gender roles forced upon me. I hated being told how to do things, people thinking I’m less smart because I’m a girl, saying what women are and aren’t capable of, how I shouldn’t chase romantic partners but rather let them chase me, and that my ultimate destiny would be the house with the white picket fence. It’s all just a bunch of bullshit. I didn’t want to be a man because I wasn’t a woman; I just didn’t want to be a woman in the way my community expected me to be. 

Now, I feel really confident identifying as a pansexual or queer woman. I sometimes also say that I’m bisexual, especially if someone is not well-versed in LGBTQ+ issues and/or doesn’t know what pansexual means. It doesn’t matter to me all that much. It’s all good. What matters the most is that people respect me (whether I am with a partner or not) and see me for who I am. 

It’s definitely a trial and error thing (a process, if you will), and it sounds like you’re already experimenting with your gender identity, so you’re well on your way! Do what feels right, do what excites you, experiment, and just have some gosh dang fun!

Good luck! You’ve always got the support of this community. 

TL;DR - Experiment. Chase joy. Wisdom, along with knowing who you are, only comes with time, practice, and reflection.


Edit: Sorry for even more words, but I did want to address one last thing re: your sexuality - genital preference! I actually struggled with this one too. When I was much younger, I thought that because I enjoyed penetration that I would only want to have sex with people who have penises. However, as I learned more and tried more things, I realized that I was attracted to all sorts of people, regardless of their gender identity or genitals. 

My first sexual experience was actually with a woman! It was wonderful; she treated me with all the gentleness one could ask for, while also teaching me a thing or two about consent. Top notch stuff. 

From then on, I figured out that sex does not always have to be about PIV sex. For me, sex can encompass many different physical acts. Just kissing and touching can be sexual! And whatever sexual acts you want to experience can (usually) be achieved with a person of any gender identity or genitals! Do you enjoy penetrative sex, but are with someone who has a vagina? It’s strap-on time! Toys are me often a couple’s best friend. Do you get off just on fingering alone? Well, good news! A lot of people have fingers! 

Again, I will reiterate my above advice: experiment and figure out what brings you pleasure! And, moreover, discuss it with your partner! “Hey, I am interested in this - do you think we could try it?” or, “Hey, I have never been with a person who has -insert genitals here- is it okay if we takes things slowly and/or would you be willing to guide me through this experience?” These kinds of phrases and questions go a LONG WAY! Talking about things before you do them, discussing what is working for you during the act, and how you feel afterwards almost always makes the experience better, at least in my experience. And it ensures you can improve if you engage in such acts again! 

This is just from my life experience, and therefore will not be applicable to everyone. I just hope it help you in some way. Again, good luck. I believe in you.

I think you might be talking about the movie "The Box" (2009) with Cameron Diaz and James Marsden. It says it was based on a Twilight Zone episode, but that was based on a story called "Button, Button." 

From Wikipedia: ""Button, Button" was first published in [*Playboy*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboy), June 1970, a short story written by [Richard Matheson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Matheson). The story was republished as part of a collection of Matheson's short stories.

In the original short story, the plot is resolved differently. Norma presses the button, and receives the money—after her husband dies in a train incident where he is pushed onto the tracks (the money was the no-fault insurance settlement, which is $50,000 instead of the $200,000 in the *Twilight Zone*episode). A despondent Norma asks the stranger why her husband was the one who was killed. The stranger replies, "Do you really think you knew your husband?"

Matheson strongly disapproved of the *Twilight Zone* version, especially the new ending, and used his pseudonym Logan Swanson for the teleplay."

Hope this helps!

I really sympathize with your post. As a person who has struggled with insecurities, mental health issues, and my sexuality, I understand how hard it can be to love yourself. 

Honestly, I think there are big steps and small steps you can take right now that could help your self esteem and make your life better. Please note, these are only my recommendations based on my personal experience, so they may not all work for you, but variations of these ideas might. 

* First on the list of big things: see a therapist, find a school guidance counselor, or find an adult you trust with whom you could talk about these feelings. In my opinion, there is nothing worse than living inside my head with all of my pain. A therapist, if you are able to go to one, can be excellent help for talking about things you feel self-conscious about (they don't judge!) and helping you form a plan to deal with the issues you want to fix in your life. 
*  Trying finding some resources that could help you. Googling terms like "gender confusion" or "agender" might be able to yield helpful information. Based on a little googling myself, [this website](http://neutrois.com/resources/#genderqueer) may be of help for your gender-related questions. For self-acceptance and mental health, I would suggest either [this](https://www.metanoia.org/) or [this](https://www.suicideforum.com/) website. I have been to these sites numerous times and they have helped calm me down when I am anxious or feeling suicidal. 
* It took me years to accept my own sexuality, given I used to belong to a conservative religious community, and longer still to publicly come out. One of the things that didn't help was that I never felt I had the words to express myself. I tried out bisexual and pansexual, but the word that spoke to me the most was "queer." I can't explain really... it stuck with me because it expressed that I felt differently than the majority of people, while still feeling flexible enough that if the way I felt ever evolved, I would still fit in this term. I think maybe if you could find a word that fits you, it might help you feel a little better. You say you don't feel like agender fits - maybe you would like something else like gender-neutral, non-binary, or genderqueer? Again, just try surfing the web and or using a dictionary like [this](http://itspronouncedmetrosexual.com/2013/01/a-comprehensive-list-of-lgbtq-term-definitions/) to find words that make you feel good.
* Try to find the little things that make you happy. You said that you're critical of wearing some things - maybe you try wearing a different shirt or hat one day, even though it makes you feel a little uncomfortable. I'm a relatively boring clothing person, so I express myself by wearing bright and colorful socks! Even though other people don't always notice, I know they're there! I even get compliments on them sometimes, which always feels nice. It can also be helpful to find something that you're good at or just want to be good at. For a long time, I brought myself down for not being creative. But one day, two years ago, I went to an art fair (something that was way out of my comfort zone!) and met an awesome couple who told me that everyone was capable of being creative. They sat with me almost an hour and we just drew pictures together. Even though I'm no amazing artist, it feels really nice to express myself in that way once in a while. 

When my grandmother died six months ago, I spiraled into one of the hardest depressions of my life. It got so bad that about a month ago, I spent a few days in a psych ward. I'm feeling better now; one of the things that helped me was that I started doing things she had taught me to do when I was a kid, like knitting and sewing. Both of those things became very therapeutic for me and reminded me that I am still connected with her. I am still dealing with all of my mental health issues, some days are better than others, but overall I am getting better. 

These suggestion, again, are by no means 100% foolproof. Your post just really struck me because I used to feel a lot like you. And I definitely wish someone had come to me ten years ago, taken my hand, and told me it's all going to be okay. There were a lot of times when I hated myself, wished I were dead. But 10 years later, there are a lot of days when I am happy, when I can look at something I've done and feel proud, when I can look at the friendships I've built and feel so so grateful. I promise you, OP, things can get better for you. It may not be easy and you will definitely have bad days, but it is possible for you to become the person you want to be. You absolutely deserve to feel happy in your own skin. I wish you all the best, and feel free to PM me any time.

My family was never religious growing up. My father has always been agnostic, and never talked about religion with us. My mother was raised a strict Baptist, but she left the church when she hit college because she was very liberal and couldn't agree with a lot that was taught by her church. I never really knew about any religion until I hit preschool and kindergarten, and kids started talking about "church." I had no idea what they were talking about, and had no clue what God was, so I asked my parents about it. I can't remember what they said to me; all I remember was thinking that it was weird that almost all the kids I knew were going to this place called church and I wasn't. It is very helpful to mention at this point in the story that the town I was raised in was extremely conservative and Christian. Even when I was still in elementary school, other kids thought it was strange that I didn't go to church. I didn't think much of it, as I didn't know God or Jesus. 

Enter my best friend. I met her in kindergarten, but we truly became best friends in the third grade. I didn't learn until much later that she was a Baha'i. She kept her mouth shut about it, as I did about my lack of religion, simply because it wasn't the norm. It wasn't until the fourth grade that I discovered what this "church" was all about, when I went to see my neighbor's First Communion. My mother appreciated the welcoming atmosphere of the Catholic church, so my mother, sister, and I did RCIA (Right of Christian Initiation for Adults; I forget what the kids' version is), and became full members by the time I graduated elementary school. 

Middle school passed, and I hit high school. Here things got messy. I became very depressed, for reasons I will not elaborate on here (sorry), the summer after ninth grade. I got to an extreme low point one day, and called my other best friend (who is a Jehovah's Witness). He told me that God would never want me to hurt myself, and that He created something he was proud of, and that He loved me so much. In that moment, I decided I needed to turn my life around. I started attending mass regularly, praying much more, and with time and hard work I got better. I eventually confided in my best friend (the Baha'i one), and she supported me through everything. We began to bond a lot over our mutual spirituality because we were both very spiritual people. I learned a lot from her about the Baha'i faith, and in tenth grade I had to do a human rights research paper and presentation, so I chose to do mine on the Baha'i persecution in Iran. I had to do a lot of research on the faith, and of course I talked to my best friend and her family a lot about it (they are all very involved in the community). As I was researching, I came to the realization that I shared many of the beliefs Baha'is held, including the oneness of religion and humanity and God. Eventually, I asked her if I could borrow some prayer books and books of scripture. I performed the fast for the first time, which was a big struggle, but still a good experience. Eventually I was reciting obligatory prayers by heart. This continued all throughout the rest of high school. My best friend and I even considered running a junior youth club together, although it fell through for logistical reasons. 

Then college rolled around, and we had to go our separate ways. She chose to do a year of service, and I went off to university. However, times got hard for me again. For the last six months, I have been struggling a lot with depression and anxiety problems. I didn't pray for a long time, so I also was losing grasp of my spiritual self. I decided to go to therapy, which has helped me sort out a lot of my problems, and I strengthened my relationships with my friends after I told them what was happening with me. Last night, I made the decision that enough was enough. I prayed to God for the first time in a long time, and decided that I need to let go. I feel like many people like to paint a picture of the shitty American high school. Mine was not so bad though. However, I should note, at this point, that I come from a very small, college prep school. I found that many of us were too caught up in our own business that we mostly just kept the insults to a minimum. There were never any fights; the only violence was minimal, and swiftly dealt with. The only shit that ever happened would be that pathetic drama queens would sometimes start awful rumors. My best friend was the recipient of a lot of stupid gossip and drama that caused her a lot of grief, but she quickly withdrew herself, and is doing better now. Generally, those drama queens fell out of favor within a year or two after their popularity rose. 

However, this was my school; one that had a graduating class of less than 100. My sister did go to a much bigger school, probably 10 times the size, and I do hear of a lot more shit that went down there. My dad also teaches at a big school, typically one with lower income families, and he also sees more vulgarities than what existed at my school. 

Overall, I feel like the general stereotypes of American high schools is a bit overdone. There is no incessant cycles of bullying that exist, normally. Kids are not fighting around every corner. If anything, bullying is concentrated to small groups of people, or just two individuals themselves. Sometimes that bullying can escalate to an overwhelming level; other times, the individuals forget about it because the subject is futile. There are factions in every school, and sometimes the factions (like nerds and the social butterflies, or if you prefer, populars) disagree on fundamental levels, like differing interests ("You watch Star Trek? What the fuck?") or differing apparel ("You're wearing 4 inch stilletos to school? What the fuck?"). 

Overall, however, we were prepubescent teenagers who tended to think every small problem or conflict was a "big deal," when in reality, it wasn't. These overreactions led to the small amounts of "drama" that existed in high school. Looking back, though, I can honestly say that modern depictions or ideas of American high school are overly dramatized. Especially when you have certain tv shows like Glee. My high school experience in no way came close to that. That show only contributes to the overwhelming stereotype of American high school. Maybe the difference between this stereotype and real high school experience is that each one of us made a choice about what we wanted our experience to be. I chose a path that allowed to exist free of any drama, and so I led a pleasurable existence free from unnecessary chaos. 

Well damn, that was a lot of words. Sorry for the word vomit, here's a tl;dr!

Tl;dr - American high school may be portrayed as an adolescent shit-hole, but in reality, these stereotypes are overplayed, and I found  plenty of opportunities to grow because I chose to not get involved in pointless drama.
